standard.title: Language in formal and informal contexts
standard.description: explore language used to develop relationships in formal and informal situations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how cooperation depends on shared social conventions that vary with formality (AC9E3LA01). They have not yet explored how language relationships vary across formal/informal contexts and how cultural background influences interaction.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify how language choices — including register, vocabulary and inclusive phrasing — vary across formal and informal situations, and explain how factors such as age, expertise, familiarity and cultural background shape these choices.

nodes.label: Register and formality
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that language changes depending on whether a situation is formal or informal, and give examples of the same idea expressed in each register.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of formal and informal language in a provided text or scenario and explain why the register differs.
nodes.typical_width: Compare formal and informal language across two or more familiar contexts (e.g. playground vs classroom report) and identify specific features — vocabulary choices, sentence structure, tone — that signal formality.
wider: Compare written formal and informal registers in the same genre across different purposes, such as a formal letter vs a text message covering the same request
Examine how digital communication contexts (email, chat, social media) sit on the formality spectrum and what signals register in each
nodes.hinge_reason: N2's analysis of how factors like age and expertise shape language choices requires students to understand register as contextually appropriate — without dispelling the formal=correct misconception, N2 analysis produces distorted conclusions about why language varies.

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate formal language with 'correct' language and informal with 'wrong'. Encountering multiple contexts where informal register is appropriate — and where formal register would be odd — helps displace this misconception.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The formality spectrum is genuinely variable across contexts. Wider engagement produces richer understanding of register as a continuum rather than a binary.
success_criteria: Can identify a formal and an informal version of the same communicative act and name at least one language feature that marks the difference
Does not treat formal language as simply 'more correct' — can explain that both registers serve different purposes

nodes.label: Factors shaping language choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how age, expertise and familiarity between speakers influence language choices in an interaction.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how one factor (e.g. talking to an expert vs a peer) changes the language used in a specific interaction.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse interactions across at least two relationship types (adult/child, expert/novice, friend/friend) and describe how each factor shapes vocabulary, tone and degree of formality.
wider: Compare how the same information is communicated differently depending on the audience's expertise — such as a scientist explaining an idea to colleagues versus to primary students
Examine how familiarity changes language over time in a relationship, using text-based examples such as letter exchanges or dialogue sequences
success_criteria: Can name at least two factors (age, expertise, familiarity) that influence language choices and link each to a concrete example
Can explain why the same person might use different language in two different relationships

nodes.label: Inclusive language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify inclusive and non-inclusive language choices and explain why inclusive language matters in different contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one example of inclusive language and explain why it is used rather than an alternative phrasing.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise inclusive language principles in a range of texts and contexts, including gender-neutral terms, respectful naming and avoiding assumptions; explain the relational purpose of inclusive choices.
wider: Explore how language expectations around inclusion have changed over time by comparing older texts with contemporary equivalents
Research language used in formal contexts such as school communications or public signage, identifying where inclusive language is and is not used and suggesting revisions
success_criteria: Can identify a non-inclusive phrasing and suggest an inclusive alternative with a reason
Understands that inclusive language is a relational choice, not just a rule

nodes.label: Cultural conventions in interaction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how greeting conventions and respectful forms of address vary across cultures, including First Nations Australian practices.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least one cultural convention that shapes how people greet or address each other formally.
nodes.typical_width: Compare greeting and address conventions across at least two cultural contexts, including First Nations Australian conventions for respecting Elders, and explain how these reflect cultural values about relationships.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian protocols for greeting, introducing and acknowledging Country and Elders, and compare these with conventions in other cultural groups represented in the class community
Investigate how formal greetings and terms of address differ across a range of cultures represented in Australian society and discuss what these differences reveal about values and relationships

response_modes.reason: Without encountering diverse examples, students default to a single cultural norm as the standard. Multiple cultural contexts help students understand conventions as culturally situated rather than universal.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australian protocols and cross-cultural conventions offer rich inquiry opportunities beyond minimum. Engaging this node widely builds genuine intercultural understanding.
success_criteria: Can describe at least one First Nations Australian convention for greeting or addressing Elders and explain its cultural significance
Does not treat one cultural convention as the default — can explain that conventions reflect cultural values
